```{r setup}
library(StressSystems)
```

## The stress-strength model

A component with random strength $X$ is exposed to a random stress $Y$. It
survives as long as the stress does not exceed the strength, so its
reliability is

$$R = P(Y < X).$$

StressSystems computes $R$ for any pair of independent continuous
distributions, estimates it from data, and extends it to systems of several
components or several stresses. The general version used throughout the
package scales the stress by a constant $c > 0$, giving $R = P(cY < X)$.
With $c = 1$ (the default) this is the usual model; $c > 1$ means the stress
is amplified and $c < 1$ that it is attenuated.

A typical workflow has three steps:

1. describe the strength and stress distributions with `ss_dist()`;
2. compute $R$ for known parameters with `ss_R()` or one of the system
   functions;
3. estimate $R$ from samples with `ss_estimate_R()`, or study estimators by
   simulation with `ss_simulate()`.

## Step 1: describing a distribution

`ss_dist()` turns a distribution into an object the rest of the package can
use. There are three ways to call it.

**Built-in families.** The package ships the Topp-Leone distribution on
$(0, 1)$ and the two-parameter generalized Rayleigh (Burr type X)
distribution:

```{r}
TL <- ss_dist("toppleone")
GR <- ss_dist("genrayleigh")
TL
GR
```

**Any R family, by name.** For a name such as `"weibull"`, `ss_dist()` looks
up `dweibull()`, `pweibull()`, `qweibull()` and `rweibull()` and reads the
parameter names from the arguments of the density. Any family that follows
R's `d/p/q/r` naming convention works this way, including families from
other packages once they are attached.

```{r}
W <- ss_dist("weibull")
W$par_names
```

For families found by name the support is guessed by evaluating the density
just outside $(0, 1)$, and a message reports the guess. Pass `lower` and
`upper` to set the support yourself and silence the message:

```{r}
E <- ss_dist("exp", lower = 0, upper = Inf)
```

When a density has both `rate` and `scale` arguments (as `dgamma()` does),
only `rate` is used as a parameter.

**User-supplied functions.** Only a density `d` and a distribution function
`p` are required. The first argument of each is the point; the remaining
named arguments are the parameters. Missing quantile and random functions
are obtained by numerically inverting `p`. Here is a power distribution
$F(x) = x^a$ on $(0, 1)$:

```{r}
dpower <- function(x, a) ifelse(x > 0 & x < 1, a * x^(a - 1), 0)
ppower <- function(q, a) pmin(pmax(q, 0), 1)^a
P <- ss_dist(d = dpower, p = ppower, lower = 0, upper = 1)
P
```

### Parameter values and constraints

Parameter values can be stored in the object with `par`, or passed later to
each function as `par_x`, `par_y`, and so on. Values passed to a function
take precedence over stored ones.

```{r}
X <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 2), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
X$par
```

Each parameter has a range, used to check values and to optimise on an
unconstrained scale during estimation. The range is known for built-in
families. Otherwise it is guessed from the parameter's name: location-type
names such as `mean`, `mu` or `location` are taken as real, `prob` as lying
in $(0, 1)$, and everything else as positive. Override a guess with
`constraints`:

```{r}
N <- ss_dist("norm", constraints = list(mean = "real", sd = "positive"),
             lower = -Inf, upper = Inf)
N$constraints
```

## Step 2: reliability for known parameters

### A single component

`ss_R()` computes $R = P(cY < X)$. For two exponential distributions with
rates 2 (strength) and 3 (stress) the exact value is $3/5$:

```{r}
X <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 2), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
Y <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 3), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
ss_R(X, Y)
ss_R(X, Y, c = 2)   # stress doubled
```

The same call works for any pair of families:

```{r}
ss_R(TL, GR, par_x = c(shape = 0.7), par_y = c(shape = 1, rate = 2))
ss_R(P, Y, par_x = c(a = 2))
```

By default the integral is computed on the probability scale,
$R = \int_0^1 F_Y(Q_X(u)/c)\,du$, whose integrand is bounded, so unbounded
densities and heavy tails cause no trouble. Without a quantile function the
density is integrated piecewise instead (`method = "density"`). If numerical
integration fails, a Monte Carlo estimate is returned with a warning.

### Several stresses

`ss_multistress()` handles a component exposed to $k$ independent stresses.
With `components = "shared"` (the default) one component must withstand all
of them; with `components = "independent"` each stress acts on its own copy
of the component. Give one row of `par_y` per stress:

```{r}
st <- data.frame(shape = c(1, 2), rate = c(2, 3))
ss_multistress(TL, GR, par_x = c(shape = 0.7), par_y = st)
ss_multistress(TL, GR, par_x = c(shape = 0.7), par_y = st,
               components = "independent")
```

The two answers differ because in the shared case every event involves the
same strength.

### A stress between two strengths

`ss_R3()` computes $P(Z < Y < X)$, the probability that the stress lies
between a lower bound $Z$ and an upper bound $X$:

```{r}
Z <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 1), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
Y <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 2), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
U <- ss_dist("exp", par = c(rate = 0.5), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
ss_R3(Z, Y, U)
2 / 2.5 - 2 / 3.5   # exact value
```

### s-out-of-k systems

`ss_sk()` gives the reliability of a system of $k$ identical, independent
components that works if at least $s$ of them exceed a common stress:

```{r}
X <- ss_dist("toppleone", par = c(shape = 0.7))
Y <- ss_dist("genrayleigh", par = c(shape = 1, rate = 2))
sapply(1:3, function(s) ss_sk(X, Y, s = s, k = 3))
```

With $s = 1$ the system is a parallel system and with $s = k$ a series
system, so reliability falls as $s$ grows.

### Cascade systems

In a cascade (standby) system with $n$ stages, stage $i$ takes over when
stage $i - 1$ fails, and its stress is scaled by $c^{i-1}$. `ss_cascade()`
returns the system reliability together with each stage's probability and
contribution:

```{r}
ss_cascade(X, Y, n = 3, c = 0.8)
```

Stages can also use different families or parameters: pass lists of
`ss_dist` objects, or one row of `par_x` and `par_y` per stage.

## Step 3: estimating R from data

### Fitting one distribution

`ss_fit()` estimates the parameters of any `ss_dist`. No starting values are
needed. The available methods are:

| method | estimator |
|---|---|
| `"mle"` | maximum likelihood, with an observed-information covariance |
| `"mps"` | maximum product of spacings |
| `"lse"`, `"wlse"` | least squares and weighted least squares on the CDF |
| `"cvm"` | Cramer-von Mises minimum distance |
| `"ad"` | Anderson-Darling minimum distance |
| `"jackknife"` | jackknife bias correction of a `base` point method |
| `"bootstrap"` | bootstrap bias correction of a `base` point method |
| `"bayes"` | Bayesian estimation by Metropolis-Hastings |

```{r}
set.seed(1)
y <- rgenrayleigh(50, shape = 1.5, rate = 2)
ss_fit(y, GR, method = "mle")
ss_fit(y, GR, method = "mps")
```

Fitting draws random starting points, so results can differ slightly between
runs. Call `set.seed()` first when you need reproducible numbers.

### Estimating R with a confidence interval

`ss_estimate_R()` fits both samples and returns the plug-in estimate of $R$.
With maximum likelihood it also gives a delta-method interval, built on the
logit scale so that it stays inside $(0, 1)$:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
x <- rtoppleone(30, shape = 0.7)
y <- rgenrayleigh(30, shape = 1, rate = 2)
ss_estimate_R(x, y, TL, GR, method = "mle")
```

Other choices of `ci` are `"boot"` (parametric bootstrap percentile
interval, available for any point method), `"bayes"` (posterior interval,
for `method = "bayes"`) and `"none"`. The fitted models are returned as
`fit_x` and `fit_y`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ss_estimate_R(x, y, TL, GR, method = "mps", ci = "boot", B = 500)
ss_estimate_R(x, y, TL, GR, method = "bayes", iter = 5000, burnin = 1000)
```

### Bayesian estimation

`ss_bayes()` runs a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler. The prior is a
function of the named parameter vector that returns the log prior density on
the natural scale; the default `NULL` is a flat prior. For example,
independent Gamma(1, 1) priors on every parameter:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prior <- function(th) sum(dgamma(th, 1, 1, log = TRUE))
ss_estimate_R(x, y, TL, GR, method = "bayes", prior = prior,
              iter = 5000, burnin = 1000)
```

The posterior draws of each fit are in `fit_x$draws` and `fit_y$draws`, the
draws of $R$ in `draws`, and an HPD interval for $R$ in `hpd`.

## Monte Carlo studies

`ss_simulate()` repeatedly draws samples from known distributions, estimates
$R$ with each method and summarises bias, mean squared error, interval
coverage and interval length. Failed replications are counted in the
`failed` column rather than dropped silently.

```{r}
sim <- ss_simulate(TL, GR, par_x = c(shape = 0.7),
                   par_y = c(shape = 1, rate = 2),
                   n = c(10, 30), MC = 20, methods = c("mle", "mps"),
                   seed = 1)
sim
```

Per-parameter results are in `sim$parameters`, and every replication in
`sim$raw`. A realistic study uses `MC = 1000` or more. `ss_simulate_grid()`
runs the same study over every combination of rows of two parameter grids
and stacks the results, with the true parameters as leading columns. A
complete example script is installed with the package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
file.show(system.file("scripts", "toppleone_genrayleigh_study.R",
                      package = "StressSystems"))
```

On Linux and macOS, `cores > 1` runs replications in parallel forked
processes. In this version, results with `cores > 1` are not exactly
reproducible from `seed`; use `cores = 1` when you need identical numbers
across runs.

## Things to know

* The built-in `d/p/q/r` functions accept a vector of points but a single
  value of each parameter, so `dtoppleone(0.5, shape = c(1, 2))` is an
  error. Use `sapply()` over parameter values instead.
* `qtoppleone()` and `qgenrayleigh()` return `NaN`, with a warning, for
  probabilities outside $[0, 1]$.
* The generalized Rayleigh distribution here has
  $F(x) = (1 - e^{-(\lambda x)^2})^{\alpha}$ with `shape` $= \alpha$ and
  `rate` $= \lambda$. `VGAM::dgenray()` uses `scale` $= 1/\lambda$.
* All variables are assumed independent.
